title: Northminster Presbyterian Church
metaTitle: Northminster Presbyterian Church — Church Website · Artifact Digital
description: A neighborhood church website built around the first-time visitor: the service time and directions on every screen, a visit page that answers the unglamorous questions, and the congregation’s own photography instead of stock.

card.blurb: A neighborhood church in Clairemont since 1953, rebuilt around the question a newcomer actually has: what happens if I show up?
card.imageAlt: Two phone screens from the Northminster site over a woman seated in the sanctuary during a Sunday service.

lede: Northminster is a small Presbyterian church in Clairemont — about sixty people on a Sunday, in the same tented sanctuary they broke ground on in the sixties. The website’s job isn’t to explain a denomination. It’s to get a stranger from “maybe” to a seat.
pillarsHeading: A church website gets read by someone standing outside.

pillars.title: The real questions are logistical
pillars.body: When does it start, how long is it, where do I park, what happens to my kids, will I be the only one who doesn’t know anyone. A site organised around ministries and committees answers none of that — and those are the questions that decide whether someone comes.

pillars.title: Sixty people and no web team
pillars.body: A congregation this size has no communications staff. The structure has to stay right when nobody is tending it, and adding a sermon or an event can’t require a developer.

pillars.title: The decision happens on a phone
pillars.body: Someone looks up a church on a Saturday night, or at eight on a Sunday morning in their kitchen. A site that makes them hunt for the service time is answering the wrong question slowly.

storyHeadingLines.text: The site isn’t about the church.
It’s the first five minutes of a visit.

storyParagraphs: So the newcomer’s three facts lead everywhere: the service time and address in the header, “Plan your visit” following down the page, and a bar pinned to the bottom of every phone screen with the hour, directions and a number that dials. The visit page answers the unglamorous things — one service, about an hour, kids from three through sixth grade, coffee before and after.

The photography is theirs, not stock: their kitchen on a Wednesday night, their garden, their sanctuary. And the church is marked up as a place with a weekly service schedule, so a search for a church nearby gets back the right hour and the right address.
storyImageAlt: The Northminster homepage on a laptop and a phone: “There’s room at the table.”
storyCaption: The same three facts lead on every screen: when, where, and what to do next.

highlights.title: The answer before the ask
highlights.body: Service time, address and directions in the header, in the footer, and pinned to the bottom of every phone screen with a tap-to-call number.

highlights.title: Written for a first Sunday
highlights.body: A visit page about the hour itself — how long it runs, where the kids go, what the music is like — rather than a statement of beliefs.

highlights.title: Their own faces
highlights.body: The congregation’s photographs throughout: the Wednesday night kitchen, the community garden, the sanctuary, the people who fill them.

highlights.title: Findable on a Sunday morning
highlights.body: Marked up as a church with a service schedule and a mapped location, so local search can return the right hour and address.

highlights.title: Light enough for a small church
highlights.body: A static build with the stylesheet inlined and every photograph generated at six sizes, so it stays quick on a phone with one bar of signal.

ctaHeading: Need a site that does the welcoming for you?

feature.alt: Four phone screens from the Northminster site — the hero, plan your visit, the leadership page and the menu — over a Sunday service in the sanctuary.
feature.caption: How most people meet the church: on a phone, about a room they haven’t walked into yet.

problem: Turning a first visit into something a stranger can picture
